text: {"answer": "Evidence leans toward remote work being neutral to positive for productivity, but the effect depends on conditions. Supporting studies report gains: a Saudi financial-sector study found remote work positively associated with worker productivity through job satisfaction and work-life balance [d3dba06e800d#2], and a field experiment found remote working generally increased job performance, most strongly for mothers [ef88116f982d#1]. A meta-style summary of 50+ studies reports a median +10% for focused tasks but -4% for collaborative tasks, and a Trip.com randomized trial found hybrid schedules showed no measurable productivity difference from in-office peers [d658dc380b73#5]. The contradicting side is real: a panel survey of 3,123 Japanese office workers found full-remote work (five days a week) was associated with reduced work productivity and higher presenteeism, even though remote work reduced stress [abefd158b9c2#2][abefd158b9c2#0]. Conscientiousness also predicts higher self-reported WFH productivity, suggesting individual differences matter [44ecc13330bd#0]. Overall, the balance suggests partial or hybrid remote work can help, while full-time remote work may hurt, with moderate confidence.", "confidence": 60, "one_line": "Mixed evidence: remote or hybrid work often matches or raises productivity, but full-time remote may reduce it and effects depend on task and person."}
